386.title: The donkey speaks (Numbers 22)
386.hook: a prophet for hire is stopped by his own donkey
386.howItsDone: The Rule of Saint Benedict tells the abbot to call the whole community together for important matters, because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger, and Benedictine communities still hold such councils.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spies: twelve saw the same land, ten saw giants, two said we can. Your line was we are able.

Yes, the Bible has a talking donkey, and the story is funnier than its reputation. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, and Moab's king, Balak, is terrified. He can't beat them in battle, so he sends for a famous seer named Balaam, a man whose curses were said to stick, and offers him a fortune to curse Israel. Balaam is the one person in the story who's supposed to see what others can't. Hold onto that. Because on the road to Moab, the only one who sees anything is his donkey.
screen: `A FRIGHTENED KING.` → `A SEER FOR HIRE.` → `ONLY THE DONKEY SEES.`

segments.voice: First, the road. An angel of the Lord stands in the road with a drawn sword. Balaam doesn't see it. The donkey does, and swerves into a field. He beats her back onto the road. Then a narrow path between vineyard walls; the angel again; the donkey presses against the wall and crushes Balaam's foot. He beats her again. Then a spot so narrow there's no way around, and the donkey simply lies down under him. Furious, he beats her with his staff. Second, the voice. God opens the donkey's mouth, and she asks: what have I done to you, that you've struck me these three times? Balaam, without blinking, argues with her: you've made a fool of me; if I had a sword I'd kill you. And she says, roughly: am I not your donkey, the one you've ridden all your life? Have I ever done this to you before? He has to admit it. No. Third, the eyes. Only then does God open Balaam's eyes, and he sees the angel and falls on his face. The famous seer couldn't see what was in front of his own animal. Fourth, how it ends. Balaam goes on to Moab, and every time he opens his mouth to curse Israel, a blessing comes out, including a line about a star rising out of Jacob, which Christian readers link to the star the Magi followed. The man hired to curse can't stop blessing. Saint Benedict, writing his rule for monks, told the abbot to hear even the youngest, because God often shows what is better to them.
screen: `THE ANGEL ONLY THE DONKEY SEES.` · `WHAT HAVE I DONE TO YOU?` · `THEN BALAAM'S EYES ARE OPENED.` · `A CURSE THAT COMES OUT A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Think of a voice you've brushed off lately: your kid, the quiet coworker, someone younger or less important than you, or even your own body swerving off the road, the headache, the tiredness. What has it been saying? Don't argue the way Balaam did; just hear it out. If you pray, ask God to open your eyes; if not, give that voice two full minutes.
Balaam, a seer for hire who couldn't see the angel in the road, though his own donkey could, and said so. Today's word.
Your line: even the donkey knew. Sometimes the warning comes from the least likely place. That's day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4–9)
387.hook: love the Lord with all thy heart, soul and strength; Jesus calls it the first commandment
387.howItsDone: In the Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer on Saturday evening includes Deuteronomy 6:4–7, and the Catechism opens its teaching on the first commandment with Jesus's words, love the Lord your God with all your heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the donkey that saw the angel when the famous seer, Balaam, couldn't. Your line was even the donkey knew.

Forty years have passed. The generation that left Egypt is almost gone. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from the land, and Moses, old now, gives one long last speech: the book of Deuteronomy. In the middle of it he says one sentence so central that it's been prayed every morning and every night for many centuries. When Jesus is asked which commandment is the greatest of all, he doesn't make up a new answer. He quotes this.
screen: `FORTY YEARS LATER.` → `MOSES'S LAST SPEECH.` → `ONE SENTENCE, PRAYED TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. It begins with a command: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord." In Hebrew, the first word is shema, hear, and that's what the whole prayer is called. Not believe, not think about. Hear. Listening is where it starts. Second, the love. "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength." Heart, in Hebrew thinking, is where you decide, not only where you feel. Soul is your life itself. And strength is a word that usually means very or exceedingly: love God with all your muchness, everything you've got. Third, the places. These words shall be in your heart, Moses says. Teach them to your children. Talk about them at home and on the road, lying down and getting up. Bind them on your hand and between your eyes; write them on the doorposts. Jews still do this: the small scroll on the doorframe, the mezuzah, and the leather boxes called tefillin worn in morning prayer. They still pray the Shema morning and night; for many, it is the last thing they hope to say. Fourth, Jesus. When a scribe asks him which commandment is first of all, Jesus answers, in Mark's Gospel, beginning with these same words, hear, O Israel, and then adds a second from Leviticus: love your neighbor as yourself. In Matthew he calls the first the greatest. Catholics pray the Shema too. Every Saturday night, the Church's Night Prayer reads these verses from Deuteronomy, at the very hour Moses names: when you lie down.
screen: `SHEMA: HEAR.` · `HEART, SOUL AND STRENGTH.` · `AT HOME, ON THE ROAD, ON THE DOOR.` · `JESUS: THE FIRST COMMANDMENT.`

segments.voice: Start where the prayer starts: for a minute, just listen, to the room, your breath, the silence underneath. Then, if you pray, say the words slowly: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord; thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength. If you don't pray, ask instead what you love with your whole heart.
Shema. Hebrew for hear: the first word of Israel's great prayer, love God with heart, soul and strength, which Jesus called the first commandment. Today's word.
Your line: with all thy heart. First hear, then love. Day three hundred eighty-seven, done.

388.title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
388.hook: life and death set before you: choose life
388.carry: the word is very near you
388.howItsDone: Deuteronomy 30:15–20 is read at Mass on the Thursday after Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, and Pope John Paul II's encyclical Evangelium Vitae (1995) draws on it in teaching the dignity of every human life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema: hear, O Israel, and love God with heart, soul and strength. Your line was with all thy heart.

The day after Ash Wednesday, when Catholics have just had ashes on their foreheads and heard remember you are dust, the Church opens the Bible to this page. Moses is near the end of his last speech. He's given all the laws, the stories, the warnings. Now he does what a good teacher does at the end of a long course: he boils it down to one choice. Not a hundred rules. Two roads. And in front of witnesses, he tells them which one to take.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `THE END OF MOSES'S SPEECH.` → `TWO ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, the nearness. Just before this, Moses says this commandment isn't too hard for you or far away. It isn't up in heaven, so that you'd need someone to go get it, and it isn't across the sea. The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it. Second, the choice. "I call heaven and earth to witness this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Moses doesn't pretend there's no choice, and he doesn't make it for them. He lays both roads out plainly and then, like a parent, can't help saying which one he hopes they'll take. Third, what life means. In Hebrew, the word for life, chayyim, is plural, as if life were never just one thing; the toast l'chaim, to life, comes from it. And Moses says what that life is: loving the Lord, listening to his voice, holding fast to him, for he is your life and the length of your days. Choosing life, in Moses's words, isn't only staying alive. Fourth, how Catholics carry it. Pope John Paul the Second drew on passages like this in his letter on the Gospel of Life, teaching that every human life, from its beginning to its natural end, is a gift to protect. And the Church puts this reading at the start of Lent, a season of small choices, every one of them a road.
screen: `THE WORD IS VERY NEAR YOU.` · `LIFE AND DEATH, BLESSING AND CURSE.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, IN THE PLURAL.` · `HE IS THY LIFE.`

segments.voice: Look at the day ahead and find one small fork in it: bed on time or scrolling till two, calling your mother back or letting it go another week, the kind word or the sharp one. See both roads clearly, the way Moses laid them out, and choose the one with more life in it. If you pray, ask for help to keep that choice; if not, commit to it quietly.
Choose life. Moses's final charge: life and death set before you, and a plea to choose life, and the God who is life. Today's word.
Your line: the word is very near you. Close enough to choose today. Day three hundred eighty-eight, in the books.

389.title: Moses on Nebo (Deuteronomy 34)
389.hook: he sees the promised land and dies before entering
389.howItsDone: Catholics honor Moses as a holy prophet, and pilgrims visit Mount Nebo in Jordan, where a Franciscan-cared-for church and lookout stand over the Jordan valley, though the text says no one knows where Moses is buried.

segments.voice: Yesterday, choose life: two roads, and Moses pleading for one. Your line was the word is very near you.

An old man climbs a mountain alone. Behind him, in the plains of Moab, a whole people waits. He has walked with them through a sea, a desert, a golden calf, a long run of complaints and a long run of mercies. At the top of Nebo, God shows him everything: the hills of the north, the far sea in the west, the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees. And then God tells him plainly: you have seen it with your eyes. You will not go over.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CLIMBS NEBO.` → `THE WHOLE LAND IN VIEW.` → `YOU WILL NOT GO OVER.`

segments.voice: First, why. Back in the book of Numbers, at a place called Meribah, the people were dying of thirst, and God told Moses to speak to a rock. Moses, angry, struck it twice instead. Water came. But God told him then: you won't bring this people into the land. Readers still argue about why that moment counted so much. The text doesn't fully explain it. Second, the death. The text says Moses the servant of the Lord died there, according to the word of the Lord. In Hebrew, literally, at the mouth of the Lord; Jewish tradition came to say God took his soul with a kiss. He was a hundred and twenty, and his eye was not dim. God himself buries him, and no one knows his grave to this day. Third, the people. They weep for him thirty days. Joshua, full of the spirit of wisdom, takes over. And the book closes: there never arose again a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face. Fourth, how the story goes on. One opinion in the Talmud says Joshua wrote these last verses, since Moses couldn't describe his own burial. The Gospels bring Moses back once more, on a mountain inside the land, talking with Jesus at the Transfiguration; Luke says they spoke of the exodus Jesus would accomplish in Jerusalem. And the night before he was killed in 1968, Martin Luther King Junior told a church in Memphis he had been to the mountaintop and seen the promised land, and might not get there with them.
screen: `STRIKING THE ROCK AT MERIBAH.` · `HE DIES AT THE MOUTH OF THE LORD.` · `NO ONE KNOWS HIS GRAVE.` · `NO PROPHET LIKE MOSES.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're working toward that is bigger than your lifetime: a child growing up, a parish, a cause, a family healing that may take generations. Picture the far end of it; let yourself want it, and gently accept that you may only see it from the mountain. If you pray, entrust it to God, who buried Moses himself; if not, hold it with open hands.
Nebo. The mountain where the prophet the Lord knew face to face was shown the whole promised land, and died before he could enter it. Today's word.
Your line: some only see it. Seeing it from the mountain doesn't make your part smaller. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

390.title: Rahab (Joshua 2; 6)
390.hook: a woman on the wall hides the spies and hangs a scarlet cord; she's named in Jesus's family tree
390.tomorrow: as for me and my house
390.howItsDone: Catholics hear Rahab's name in the genealogy of Jesus from Matthew 1, read at the Christmas Vigil Mass and on December 17, and early Church writers such as Clement of Rome saw in her scarlet cord a sign of redemption through Christ's blood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses on Nebo: he saw the whole land and died before entering it. Your line was some only see it.

Remember the spies who came back saying we were like grasshoppers? A generation later, Joshua sends two more, across the Jordan to Jericho. They go to a house built right into the city wall, the house of a woman named Rahab. The Bible doesn't soften what she is: a prostitute. Someone tells the king, and his men come pounding on her door: bring out the men who came to you. She has maybe a minute to decide. And what she tells the spies afterward would have stunned that first generation: the terror of you has fallen on all of us. Our hearts melted.
screen: `TWO SPIES IN JERICHO.` → `A HOUSE IN THE WALL.` → `THE KING'S MEN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the lie and the roof. Rahab has hidden the men under stalks of flax on her roof. She tells the king's men: yes, they came, but they left at dusk; hurry and you'll catch them. The soldiers run off toward the river. Second, her confession. On the roof, she tells the spies: we heard how the Lord dried up the sea for you. Then a line of faith from someone with every reason not to have it: the Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath. She asks one thing: when you come, spare my father, my mother, my brothers and sisters. Third, the cord. She lets them down through her window on a rope. They tell her: tie this cord of scarlet thread in the window, and keep your family inside. When Jericho falls, the text says, Joshua spares Rahab and all her family, and she lives in Israel from then on. Some readers notice that the Hebrew word for this cord, tikvah, is the word used elsewhere for hope: a thread of hope hanging from a window. Saint Clement of Rome, in his letter to the Corinthians, saw in that scarlet thread a sign of redemption through the blood of Christ. Fourth, the family tree. Matthew's Gospel opens with Jesus's genealogy, and it names only a few women. Rahab is one: "Salmon begot Booz of Rahab," as the Douay-Rheims spells it. She is the mother of Boaz, who will marry Ruth. A foreigner, a prostitute, in the line of King David, and of Jesus.
screen: `HIDDEN UNDER FLAX ON THE ROOF.` · `GOD IN HEAVEN ABOVE, EARTH BENEATH.` · `TIKVAH: A CORD, A HOPE.` · `NAMED IN JESUS'S FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've filed away under a label: the neighbor with the messy past, the coworker everyone talks about, the relative who made bad choices. Ask what they might have risked that you never saw. If you pray, pray for that person by name; if not, just let the label loosen for a minute.
Rahab. The woman of Jericho who hid the spies, tied a scarlet cord in her window, and is named among Jesus's ancestors. Today's word.
Your line: the scarlet cord. A thread in a window, a family safe. See you tomorrow.

391.title: As for me and my house (Joshua 24:15)
391.hook: choose this day whom you'll serve
391.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil and on Easter Sunday, Catholics renew their baptismal promises aloud, rejecting sin and professing faith, and many Catholic families call their home a domestic church, a phrase the Catechism uses for the Christian household.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahab's thread of hope. Your line was the scarlet cord. Today, the last day of the road out of Egypt.

A plaque by a front door, or letters over a kitchen archway: as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. There it reads like a household motto. But the line was first said by an old soldier at a tense public assembly, in front of every tribe of Israel, and it was a dare. Joshua is near the end of his life. The land has been settled. And he calls everyone to a town called Shechem, to make them choose.
screen: `A PLAQUE BY THE FRONT DOOR.` → `FIRST, AN OLD SOLDIER'S DARE.` → `EVERYONE CALLED TO SHECHEM.`

segments.voice: First, Joshua retells the whole story, speaking for God: Abraham called from beyond the river, Jacob going down to Egypt, Moses and Aaron, the sea, the wilderness, a land you didn't work for, cities you didn't build, vineyards you didn't plant. Everything you have was given. Second, the choice. If serving the Lord seems wrong to you, choose this day whom you will serve: the old gods your ancestors served, or the gods of the land you're living in. Then his own answer, before anyone else's: "but as for me and my house we will serve the Lord." He goes first, and he answers for his household, not the whole nation. Third, the surprise. The people shout: we'll serve the Lord too! And Joshua says something no one expects. You can't. He is a holy God, a jealous God. It's as if he wants them to feel the weight of it, not just say yes because everyone else is. They say it again: no, we will serve the Lord. So he writes it down and sets up a great stone under an oak as a witness. Fourth, look back over the road. It began with two midwives who said no. Then a basket in the reeds, a bush that burned, a lamb and a sea, manna, Sinai and ten words, a golden calf, God's back, a blessing, a talking donkey, the Shema, choose life, Moses on Nebo, Rahab's cord. And it ends where Moses ended: with a choice that has to be made again. At Easter, the Church asks Catholics to make it again, renewing their baptismal promises out loud.

segments.voice: Bring one of your big choices to mind: a faith, a marriage, a vocation, staying sober, a promise to a friend. 392.title: Deborah under the palm (Judges 4–5)
392.hook: a prophetess judges Israel and leads the army with Barak
392.howItsDone: Catholics hear stories from Judges, among them Gideon's call, at weekday Mass in late summer of one year of the two-year cycle; Deborah's own chapters are not among those readings, so many meet her by reading the book itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua at Shechem: as for me and my house. Your line was we will serve the lord. Today, a new stretch of the book.

There's a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, between Rama and Bethel, and under it sits a woman. People come from all over Israel to bring her their quarrels: a field boundary, a stolen animal, a family feud. She listens, and she decides. The tree is so tied to her that it's called by her name: Deborah, Debbora in the Douay-Rheims. To the north, a king named Jabin has kept Israel under his thumb for twenty years with nine hundred chariots. Today we open the books of the judges and the kings, and the first person we meet under a tree is a woman.
screen: `A PALM BETWEEN RAMA AND BETHEL.` → `PEOPLE BRING HER THEIR QUARRELS.` → `TWENTY YEARS UNDER JABIN.`

segments.voice: Judge here doesn't mean a robe and a gavel. In the Book of Judges the Hebrew word is shofet: someone God raises up to lead, to rescue, and to set things right. Deborah does all of it. The Douay-Rheims introduces her this way: "Debbora a prophetess the wife of Lapidoth, who judged the people." A prophetess, so she speaks for God. A judge, so people come to her for justice. Then the crisis. She sends for a commander named Barak, Barac in the Douay, and gives him God's order: take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. Barak answers with a condition: "If thou wilt come with me, I will go: if thou wilt not come with me, I will not go." Deborah goes, but tells him the honor of the victory will fall to a woman. And it does, in a way nobody expects: the enemy general, Sisera, flees on foot and dies in the tent of another woman, Jael. Chapter five is a song, one of the oldest poems in the Bible by many scholars' reckoning, and it gives Deborah a title no general gets: "a mother arose in Israel." The Church reads this song with care. Jael's deed is violent, and the text praises it in a time of war, so Catholic readers take it as Israel's history, not a model for living. Deborah herself is remembered with honor: the leader who sat under a tree, heard her people, and went with them when they were afraid.
screen: `SHOFET — A JUDGE WHO RESCUES.` · `A PROPHETESS UNDER THE PALM.` · `IF THOU WILT COME WITH ME.` · `A MOTHER AROSE IN ISRAEL.` · then, large: `WHO JUDGED THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman who has led you somewhere: a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a boss, a nun, a coach, a neighbor who organized the whole street. Remember a time she listened, decided, or went with you when you were afraid to go alone. If you pray, thank God for her by name.
Judge. In the Book of Judges, shofet: one God raises up to lead, rescue and do justice, like Deborah under her palm. Today's word.
